title: Recognising deterioration and escalation tools
blurb: Use maternity early warning scores, NICE NG255 sepsis criteria and SBAR to recognise a woman who is becoming unwell and escalate at the right speed.
question: On day 3 after a caesarean birth, Leanne tells her community midwife she 'feels awful'. Her respiratory rate is 26, heart rate 118, BP 98/60 and temperature 35.8 °C. What should the midwife do?

teach.h: Why pregnant women can look well until they are not
teach.body: Pregnancy changes normal physiology: the baseline heart rate is 10 to 15 beats per minute higher (NG255 1.4.4), and a young, fit woman can compensate for illness or blood loss until late. Formally, an early warning score is a track and trigger tool: observations are scored so that abnormal values trigger a set response. NEWS2 is not used in pregnancy, so maternity units use a maternity early warning chart (MEWS or MEOWS); the chart in use can differ between units, so follow your local tool. In plain English: score every set of observations, and let the score and your concern start the escalation.

head: Area
High-risk finding
rows: RR 25 or more; new need for 40%+ O2 to keep sats over 92%
Systolic 90 or less (or 40 below normal); HR over 130
Mottled or ashen; cyanosis; non-blanching rash
teach.caption: NG255 table 1. Sepsis can be present without fever; ask 'could this be sepsis?'

head: Area
Moderate to high-risk finding
rows: New altered behaviour; functional decline; impaired immunity
Trauma, surgery or invasive procedure in the last 6 weeks
teach.caption: Pulse oximeters may overestimate saturations in women with darker skin (NG255 1.4.9).

children.label: Immediate senior review
children.sub: lactate, cultures; antibiotics within 1 h; fluids per lactate/BP

children.label: Bloods incl. lactate; review within 1 h
children.sub: lactate over 2 or AKI: treat as high risk

teach.caption: Fluids (16 and over): crystalloid 500 mL over less than 15 minutes, reassess, and get a consultant if no improvement after a second bolus (NG255 1.9).

letters.word: Situation: who you are, who she is, the problem now
Recommendation: what you need and by when

teach.body: The Code asks you to make a timely referral (13.2) and to act without delay if you believe there is a risk to safety (16). Record observations, scores, who you called and when, and the plan, at the time or as soon as possible (10.1). If the response does not come, escalate again up the chain. In sepsis, aim for oxygen saturations of 94-98% (NG255 1.10.1), and monitor a high-risk woman continuously or at least every 30 minutes (1.7.7).

Leanne is within 6 weeks of birth and had surgery, so she is in the high-risk group. Her RR of 26 is a high-risk criterion (25 or more); HR 118, systolic 98 and temperature 35.8 °C are moderate to high criteria. Outside hospital, any high-risk criterion means emergency transfer, usually by 999, with a pre-alert. The midwife stays with her, repeats observations, gives an SBAR handover to the paramedics and documents everything.

teach.text: A normal or LOW temperature does not rule out sepsis: a tympanic temperature under 36 °C is itself a moderate to high-risk criterion. And a heart rate that would be 'fine' for a non-pregnant adult may already be high for her, because baseline heart rate rises 10-15 beats per minute in pregnancy.

items: Use the maternity early warning chart, not NEWS2, in pregnancy; score every set of observations.
NG255 high risk: RR 25+, systolic 90 or less, HR over 130, new confusion, mottled skin, no urine 18 h.
Outside hospital, any high-risk criterion: 999 with a pre-alert.
In hospital, high risk: immediate senior review and antibiotics within 1 hour.
Escalate with SBAR, document at the time, and re-escalate if help does not come.

summary: You can now use a maternity early warning chart and the NICE NG255 criteria to judge how unwell a pregnant or recently pregnant woman is, and escalate at the right speed with SBAR. You can also explain why fever and heart rate can mislead in pregnancy.

A.q: A woman who gave birth 2 weeks ago is assessed for possible sepsis. Which finding is an NG255 HIGH-risk criterion?
options: Heart rate of 112 beats per minute
Respiratory rate of 26 per minute
Systolic blood pressure of 98 mmHg
Tympanic temperature of 35.8 °C
A.why: NG255 table 1: a respiratory rate of 25 or more is a high-risk criterion.

whyNot.0: HR 100-130 is a moderate to high-risk criterion; high risk is over 130.
whyNot.2: Systolic 91-100 is moderate to high; high risk is 90 or less.
whyNot.3: A temperature under 36 °C is a moderate to high-risk criterion.

A.q: A midwife is preparing an SBAR call to the obstetric registrar. What does the 'B' stand for?
options: Baseline observations
Breathing assessment
Background
Blood results
A.why: SBAR = Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation (NHS England SBAR guide).

whyNot.0: Observations belong in the Assessment section.
whyNot.1: Breathing findings are part of the Assessment.
whyNot.3: Blood results are part of the Assessment, not the 'B'.

A.q: When interpreting a pregnant woman's heart rate, what should the midwife remember?
options: Baseline is 10–15 bpm higher in pregnancy
Baseline is 10–15 bpm lower in pregnancy
Baseline is 30–40 bpm higher in pregnancy
Baseline heart rate is unchanged by pregnancy
A.why: NG255 1.4.4: baseline heart rate in pregnancy is 10 to 15 beats per minute higher.

whyNot.1: Heart rate rises, not falls, in pregnancy.
whyNot.2: A rise of 30-40 bpm is not normal and would suggest illness.
whyNot.3: Pregnancy does change the baseline heart rate.

B.q: On the postnatal ward, Ama meets an NG255 high-risk criterion for sepsis. When should she receive a broad-spectrum antimicrobial?
options: Within 3 hours of senior review
Within 6 hours of arrival
Once blood cultures are positive
Within 1 hour
B.why: NG255 1.7: for high-risk criteria in hospital, give a broad-spectrum antimicrobial within 1 hour, after immediate senior review and blood tests including cultures.

whyNot.0: The 3-hour window is for senior review of antibiotics in moderate-risk women without high-risk features.
whyNot.1: Six hours is far too slow for high-risk sepsis.
whyNot.2: Antibiotics must not wait for culture results.

B.q: Ruth, day 2 postnatal on the ward, has a heart rate of 115 and a respiratory rate of 22. She has no high-risk criteria. What does NG255 advise?
options: Repeat the observations in 4 hours
Bloods with lactate and review within 1 hour
Senior review of antibiotics within the next 6 hours
Discharge home with sepsis safety-netting
B.why: NG255 1.7.10: with two or more moderate to high-risk criteria, take bloods including lactate and arrange clinician review within 1 hour.

whyNot.0: Two moderate to high criteria need action within 1 hour, not routine observations.
whyNot.2: The review must be within 1 hour; 6 hours is not an NG255 time frame.
whyNot.3: Discharge is unsafe with two moderate to high-risk criteria.

B.q: A midwife is using a pulse oximeter on a woman with darker skin. What does NICE NG255 warn?
options: They read below the true value in dark skin
They read more accurately in dark skin
They are unaffected by skin colour
They may overestimate saturation
B.why: NG255 1.4.9: pulse oximeters may overestimate oxygen saturation in people with darker skin, so hypoxia can be missed.

whyNot.0: NG255 1.4.9 reports overestimation, not underestimation, in people with dark skin.
whyNot.1: Accuracy is reduced, not improved, in darker skin.
whyNot.2: Skin pigmentation can affect the reading.

C.q: Leanne is at home 3 days after a caesarean. Her RR is 26, HR 118, BP 98/60 and temperature 35.8 °C. She says she feels awful. What should the community midwife do?
options: Call 999 and pre-alert the hospital
Ask her GP to visit her later today
Advise paracetamol and review her tomorrow
Drive her to the maternity triage unit yourself
C.why: Outside hospital, any NG255 high-risk criterion (here RR 25 or more) means emergency transfer, usually by 999, with a pre-alert (1.6.1-1.6.2).

whyNot.1: A delayed GP visit is unsafe for a high-risk criterion.
whyNot.2: Paracetamol could mask fever and delay emergency care.
whyNot.3: A private car is not a safe transfer for a woman who may deteriorate en route.

C.q: Nia, day 5 postnatal, meets NG255 high-risk criteria in hospital. Her lactate is 4.5 mmol/L. Which fluid plan follows NG255?
options: 250 mL of colloid over 1 hour
1 litre of crystalloid over 4 hours as maintenance
500 mL crystalloid over less than 15 minutes
No fluids until the antibiotics are running
C.why: NG255: lactate over 4 mmol/L in high-risk sepsis needs an IV fluid bolus within 1 hour (and critical care referral): crystalloid 500 mL over less than 15 minutes, then reassess.

whyNot.0: NICE uses crystalloid boluses, not colloid over an hour.
whyNot.1: Slow maintenance fluids do not treat a lactate over 4.
whyNot.3: Fluids are given within 1 hour alongside antibiotics, not delayed.

C.q: A midwife phones the obstetric registrar about Rosa, who had a PPH yesterday and is now tachycardic and hypotensive. Which opening line best follows SBAR?
options: Rosa had a PPH of 1.5 litres yesterday after a long labour
I'm calling about Rosa, who is tachycardic and hypotensive
I think Rosa may be bleeding again and could be in shock
I need you to come and review Rosa on the ward within 10 minutes
C.why: SBAR opens with the Situation: who is calling, about whom, and the current problem. Background, Assessment and Recommendation follow.

whyNot.0: This is Background, which comes after the Situation.
whyNot.2: This is the Assessment, which follows Situation and Background.
whyNot.3: This is the Recommendation, which closes the SBAR call.

reteach.title: Count, compare, call
reteach.question: If you only had one minute with a postnatal woman, what would you count, what would you compare it with, and who would you call?

blocks.body: Count the respiratory rate for a full minute: it is often the earliest sign and the most often skipped. Compare every value with the NG255 bands and her own baseline, remembering her heart rate runs 10-15 higher in pregnancy. Then call: a high-risk criterion means senior review now in hospital, or 999 at home. Use SBAR so the person you call hears the problem first.

blocks.text: A low temperature is not reassuring: under 36 °C is a moderate to high-risk sepsis criterion.

explain.body: NG255 asks clinicians to think 'could this be sepsis?' in any pregnant or recently pregnant woman who is unwell, recognising that signs may be non-specific and she may have no fever. The high-risk group runs to 6 weeks after birth, termination or miscarriage.

items.label: after birth, termination or miscarriage: high-risk group

test.q: Which statement about sepsis in pregnancy is correct, according to NICE NG255?
options: It needs a temperature of 38 °C or above
It may be present without any fever
It is ruled out by normal saturations
It is not seen after 6 weeks postpartum
test.why: NG255 1.1: sepsis may present with non-specific signs and without fever, so a normal temperature does not exclude it.

whyNot.0: Fever is not required; a low temperature can be a sign.
whyNot.2: Normal saturations do not exclude sepsis, and oximeters can mislead.
whyNot.3: The 6-week window defines the high-risk group; sepsis can still occur later.

explain.body: Systolic 90 mmHg or less (or more than 40 below her normal) is a high-risk criterion. Systolic 91-100 is moderate to high risk (NG255 table 1).

test.q: Which systolic blood pressure is an NG255 high-risk criterion?
options: Between 91 and 100 mmHg
Between 101 and 110 mmHg
90 mmHg or less
Below 120 mmHg
test.why: NG255 table 1: a systolic BP of 90 mmHg or less (or over 40 below normal) is a high-risk criterion.

whyNot.0: 91-100 mmHg is a moderate to high-risk criterion.
whyNot.1: 101-110 mmHg is not an NG255 criterion.
whyNot.3: Below 120 mmHg is not an NG255 threshold.

explain.body: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. The recommendation says exactly what you need, such as 'please review her within 15 minutes', so the call ends with a clear plan.

test.q: In SBAR, what does the 'R' stand for?
options: Recommendation
Risk assessment
Repeat observations
Response time

whyNot.1: Risk assessment is part of the Assessment section.
whyNot.2: Repeat observations may form part of the plan, but 'R' is Recommendation.
whyNot.3: The time frame is stated within the Recommendation.

explain.body: If a pregnant or recently pregnant woman outside hospital has any high-risk criterion, NG255 advises emergency transfer, usually by 999, with a pre-alert to the receiving hospital.

test.q: A community midwife finds a woman 10 days after birth with a new altered mental state. What does NG255 advise?
options: Arrange a GP review within the next 24 hours
Repeat her observations at home in 1 hour
Advise rest, oral fluids and a call tomorrow
999 transfer with a hospital pre-alert
test.why: An objective new altered mental state is a high-risk criterion; outside hospital this means emergency transfer, usually by 999, with a pre-alert (NG255 1.6.1-1.6.2).

whyNot.0: A 24-hour GP review is far too slow for a high-risk sign.
whyNot.1: Waiting an hour at home delays emergency treatment.
whyNot.2: Home management is unsafe with a high-risk criterion.
